title: Glossary: malware, phishing, ransomware, RAT and more
body_md:
## A word is not a diagnosis

A red banner fills the browser: **“RAT detected! Zero-day infection! Call support now!”** Two alarming labels, an order and a phone number. A web page can print any words it likes without scanning a thing. Security vocabulary earns its place only when each word points at a specific mechanism, so here are the terms you will meet most, with what each one tells you and what it leaves out.

**Malware** is software or code written to do harm. **Phishing** is a deceptive attempt to make someone reveal information or do something unsafe, usually by message. The two are different things. A phishing message can lead to malware, to a fake login page or straight to a payment, and malware can arrive by routes that have nothing to do with phishing. A link isn’t malware just because you have never seen it, and a warning banner isn’t proof that anything ran. Phishing also comes with sub-labels for its aim or its delivery: *spear phishing* is tailored to one particular person, *whaling* goes after executives, and *quishing* hides the destination behind a QR code. None of these says anyone was compromised.

**Ransomware** is malicious software, or the attack built around it, that cuts you off from your data, commonly by encrypting it, and demands payment. Some criminals also steal a copy first and threaten to publish it. Whether that happened in a given incident is a question for evidence, not for the word “ransomware.” **RAT** usually stands for *remote access trojan*: malicious code that gives an outsider control of a device. A legitimate remote-support tool isn’t a RAT by nature, but handing control to a caller you haven’t verified exposes the device just the same. If you installed something at a stranger’s request, don’t guess at the category. Say what access you gave.

**Credential stuffing** is the automated replay of leaked username-and-password pairs on other services, which is why one reused password can endanger several accounts. **Business email compromise (BEC)** is fraud that rides on business messages people already trust, usually to redirect a payment. Either the mailbox has really been taken over or the sender is faked; in both cases the remedy is to confirm changed payment details by a route you already know. Phishing by text message is **smishing**, and by voice call **vishing**. The channel in the name says little about whether the message is true.

**Investment grooming** is a neutral name for what reports sometimes call “pig-butchering”: someone builds trust, introduces a supposedly profitable platform and coaxes out ever larger deposits. The nickname dehumanizes the person it describes, so with anyone who was harmed, describe the mechanism and leave it out. A **zero-day attack**, in NIST’s glossary, exploits a previously unknown vulnerability. That says nothing about price, perpetrator or likelihood. When a news story uses the term loosely, look for the vendor’s advisory before you change what you do.

### From the word to the decision

Put three questions to any alarming label: what happened, what might have been exposed, and what evidence says so. If a message announces “your account suffered a RAT and a zero-day” but wants you to call a number you don’t know and install software, those words are a claim, not proof. Open the provider’s own app or support site. If you knowingly gave someone remote control, end the session and get help from a source you trust; if a password was exposed, change it on the real service and check where else you reused it. The actions differ because the exposures differ.

Back at the red banner: no scan, no proof of infection, no named culprit. What remains is a request to call and install something, and that request is the only part that needs a decision from you.

widget_config.goal: Turn an alarming security word into what happened, what is exposed and what to do, instead of taking the word as a diagnosis.
widget_config.today_action: Take one unfamiliar term from a security advisory you trust and rewrite it as three answers: what happened, what was exposed, what I do.
widget_config.scope: A plain-language vocabulary. The people in the examples are invented. NIST definitions are technical, and what you do after an incident depends on what actually happened.

sources.title: NIST CSRC glossary: malware
sources.scope: A technical definition. A term names a category; it does not describe the state of your own device.

sources.title: NIST CSRC glossary: phishing
sources.scope: A technical definition; newer channels such as QR codes and texts may not appear in its examples.

sources.title: NIST CSRC glossary: zero-day attack
sources.scope: Definition from CNSSI 4009-2022. It makes no claim about how common these attacks are or what they cost.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Ransomware
sources.scope: A US law-enforcement overview of how ransomware works and how to respond. It is not a way to diagnose a device.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Investment Fraud
sources.scope: How US law enforcement describes it: trust built slowly, fake returns shown, small withdrawals that succeed.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4: Authenticators
sources.scope: A US technical standard written for people who build identity services; it covers how passwords are stored and the properties of authenticators.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: A US law-enforcement overview. Verifying a payment change works the same way anywhere.

sources.title: FTC: What to do if you were scammed
sources.scope: US consumer guidance sorted by what you lost or how you paid (June 2026). Your local rights may differ.

blocks.title: A siren and a “RAT detected” banner
blocks.situation: A browser page sounds a siren. Red text says a remote-access trojan has been found on Jo’s laptop, and a button tells her to call the “support” number on screen and install a screen-sharing app.
blocks.analysis: A web page can print any claim without scanning anything. The real danger is what it asks for: remote access. Jo should close the page, run the security tools she already trusts or contact the manufacturer’s support, and leave the number alone. The page diagnoses nothing.

blocks.title: A support session Jo booked herself
blocks.situation: Jo opened a ticket with her laptop’s maker through its official site. At the agreed time the support agent asks her to start the documented screen-sharing tool, and Jo can end the session whenever she likes.
blocks.analysis: Remote access can be legitimate when the person is verified, the scope is clear and the owner consents. The tool is not automatically a RAT. Jo should still keep passwords off the screen, watch what the agent does and end the access when the work is done.

blocks.title: Strip the jargon during a device scare
blocks.setup: An invented scare: a browser warning throws technical terms around. Work from what was actually exposed, not from the labels.

steps.prompt: A pop-up announces “zero-day malware detected.” What do you actually know?

choices.text: Only that the page made a claim. Check with security tools you trust.
choices.consequence: A line of web-page text stays what it is: text, not a scan report.
choices.explanation: The words don’t prove that any scan took place.

choices.text: That a nation-state attacker is inside.
choices.consequence: You have added a villain nobody has shown, and the panic that comes with one.
choices.explanation: Zero-day describes a kind of vulnerability, not who is exploiting it.

steps.prompt: The page tells you to call its number and install remote support. What do you do?

choices.text: Install the tool so the caller can confirm the alert.
choices.consequence: A stranger now has a way onto your screen, and possibly your device.
choices.explanation: Verification has to come before access. It can’t depend on it.

choices.text: Skip that contact. Close the page, and if you need help, reach the manufacturer’s support by a route you find yourself.
choices.consequence: No unknown party gets control of your device.
choices.explanation: What the page asks you to do matters more than what it calls itself.

steps.prompt: Suppose you already gave the caller control. What is the most useful thing to tell a helper?

choices.text: What ran, when, and what the caller could see. Then get help from a source you trust.
choices.consequence: A responder can judge the real exposure.
choices.explanation: Facts you observed are worth more than a guess like “RAT.”

choices.consequence: The label may be wrong, and it leaves out the details that matter.
choices.explanation: Ransomware means lost access or extortion, and neither happened here.

steps.prompt: You typed an account password while your screen was shared. What now?

choices.text: Wait for an encryption demand before doing anything.
choices.consequence: The password may already be in someone else’s hands.
choices.explanation: A stolen password is a risk with or without ransomware.

choices.text: End the session, then change that password on the real service from a device you trust, and check where else you used it.
choices.consequence: You deal with the one credential that was actually exposed.
choices.explanation: What was exposed, not how dramatic the word sounds, sets the response.

blocks.debrief: Replay it, swapping every noun for an event you actually saw. The fake warning proves no infection. A session you allowed and a password you typed on a shared screen are exposures you can name, and each has its own fix.

questions.prompt: A fake invoice email sends you to a payment page, and nothing gets installed. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: It can’t be phishing without malware.
choices.explanation: Phishing can go straight for money or credentials.

choices.text: It can be phishing with no malware at all.
choices.explanation: Phishing is the deceptive request; installing software is optional.

questions.prompt: A firm says its files are encrypted but has not confirmed that any data was stolen. What can you conclude?

choices.text: Access may be disrupted; theft would need separate evidence.
choices.explanation: Encrypting files and copying them out are two different events.

choices.text: Every ransomware attack copies every file.
choices.explanation: The word “ransomware” doesn’t prove that anything left the building.

questions.prompt: A genuine technician uses a remote-support app with the customer’s consent. Is the app automatically a RAT?

choices.text: Yes, because all remote software is malware.
No. Look at whether it was authorized and what it actually does.
choices.explanation: Remote access can be legitimate, though it still calls for care.

questions.prompt: One leaked password is tried automatically on many other sites. What is this called?

choices.explanation: Leaked login pairs get tested on other services.
No unknown software flaw is needed.
